second_order: Playing, spotting, and arguing over April Fools tricks
theme_note: Across separate exchanges, participants encounter a false death, wiki makeovers, fake levels and loot, official jokes, and one another's bait; they diagnose the trick, play along, compare it with earlier years, or complain about its effects. What varies is who authored the trick and whether the response is alarm, explanation, praise, mockery, or criticism.

second_order: Closing the Btw clan chat and Discord
theme_note: This single-code theme records the isolated report that the owner shut the clan chat and removed its Discord; it shares no demonstrated practice with the surrounding cabbage joke or canvas work.

second_order: Proposing what RuneScape should put on the canvas
theme_note: Participants turn familiar RuneScape images and sayings into candidate canvas projects. Proposals vary from A q p W, Gnome Child, Connection Lost and the construction icon to Buying GF, Grand Exchange, weapons, characters, and small additions; some are realistic, others intentionally oversized or comic.

second_order: Building from coordinates, grids, and progress calls
theme_note: Participants make proposals actionable by giving coordinates, maps, colours and sequences, recruiting clicks, reporting progress, relocating, and declaring milestones. The designs and scale vary, as do whether contributors build one image, extend it, or abandon it for a workable location.

second_order: Arguing over the pixels that make the meme right
theme_note: Participants repeatedly correct the q, C, spacing, borders, periods, colour and signature green or yellow pixels. What holds these codes together is treating tiny pixel choices as what makes the shared meme recognisable; variation lies between faithful reference, deliberate joke pixels, honest mistakes, and people undoing one another's repairs.

second_order: Fighting, bargaining, and helping across canvas borders
theme_note: Participants claim or contest space and answer neighbours through attacks, truces, permissions, treaties, relocation, restitution, and mutual aid. Some exchanges are openly hostile; others preserve a border, spare an ally, repair harm, or distinguish rogue pixels from a community's agreed position.

second_order: Praising, mocking, and disputing the canvas effort
theme_note: Participants assess what the room made and the labour it took: celebrating success and teamwork, laughing at malformed art, calling the feed spammy or the work ugly, debating whether it matters, and contrasting pride with disappointment. These are evaluations of the shared effort rather than the acts of building or defending it.

second_order: Repairing and defending the work click by click
theme_note: Participants spend scarce clicks cleaning damage, watching borders, answering attack warnings, restoring letters and images, prioritising maintenance, and recruiting relief. The work varies between routine repair, emergency defence, night shifts, manual persistence, and decisions to defer expansion because existing pieces need constant upkeep.

second_order: Moving coordination through Discord, scripts, templates, and mirrors
theme_note: Participants seek or supply coordination infrastructure beyond an ordinary post: Discords, maintenance scripts, pixel maps, reference images, livestreams, and live mirrors. These tools vary between organising people, reducing mistaken repairs, automating upkeep, and preserving a view; their unseen contents limit what can be claimed about decisions made there.

second_order: Showing the canvas work and its progress
theme_note: Participants circulate screenshots, progress logs, timelapses, status posts and terse image-led updates so others can see or recognise the work. What varies is whether the post documents a stage, points out a neighbouring image, or simply displays the current canvas without making a new call.

second_order: Explaining r/place and bringing newcomers into the work
theme_note: Participants answer what the pixel event is, explain its timer and collective art, identify the room's references, give access links, and turn explanation into an invitation or duty to help. Explanations vary from practical instructions to PvP-Microsoft-Paint metaphors and post-event accounts of what 'we' did.

second_order: Accounting for what survived when r/place ended
theme_note: After placement closes, participants publish final results, claim or divide credit, inspect defects, argue over scripts and manual labour, revisit territorial harm, and explain the event to latecomers. Celebration and criticism coexist, and retrospective claims about allies or opponents remain attributed accounts rather than a collective settlement.

second_order: Preserving and repairing the finished canvas
theme_note: Participants try to keep the completed work available or carry it into memory through screenshots, timelapses, a Minecraft replay, in-game memorial proposals, corrected final images, and submissions to a cleanup venue. Variation lies between archiving, proposing a tribute, disputing exact appearance, and repairing a final copy whose external result is unseen.

second_order: Trying to start Connection Lost again on successor canvases
theme_note: Participants propose PlaceTwo, pxls.space, a rebuilt canvas, or a generic new r/place and ask for another round. Early calls meet refusal or whitelist removal; later text reports actual sprite design on pxls.space, but completion and most off-site coordination remain unseen.
